newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Suharto urges Indonesians to vote for democracy.
newsitem.headline: Suharto urges Indonesians to vote for democracy.

text.p: President Suharto, in an election eve address, urged Indonesians to exercise their democratic rights in general elections on Thursday after a campaign marred by the worst political violence in 30 years.

"I call on all of us to exercise the right to vote with a sense of responsibility... The right to vote and the right to be elected are basic democratic political rights," he said in a nationally televised broadcast on Wednesday night.

The 27-day election campaign wound up last Friday with a peak of violence in which at least 124 people died in rioting and arson in the South Kalimantan provincial capital of Banjarmasin, according to the latest police count.

Nearly 125 million people in the world's fourth most populous nation are eligible to vote for 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives. The other 75 seats are filled by the military which does not vote.

Polls open from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. (0100-0700 GMT) with major results likely known within 24 hours. Final results will trickle in over a week from the archipelago of more than 17,500 islands stretching 5,000 km (3,000 miles) along the equator.
In the capital Jakarta, the Japanese embassy was evacuated on Wednesday morning following a hoax telephoned bomb threat.

Official sources said there had been a couple of other isolated bomb warnings and also rumours of threats in different parts of Jakarta on Tuesday. News reports said the army had arrested four men they believed were planning to set off an explosion in a north Jakarta shopping mall.
The ruling Golkar is assured of a comfortable victory in Thursday's poll, but analysts are watching the reaction to the results of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP).
The only other party legally permitted to run, the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), has been badly hit by a leadership battle and was virtually sidelined during the campaign.
Analysts are also watching for the size of Golput, or "White Party", the term used for people who spoil their ballots or abstain as a form of protest.
They said Suharto's appeal for a high turnout could reflect official concern about higher-than-usual abstentions.
Golkar officials have estimated the Golput effect in the last elections in 1992 at around three to four percent. About 90 percent of the electorate voted.

The PPP posed a strong challenge to Golkar during the campaign, in which violence was mainly between partisans of the two groups. Political analysts said further trouble might erupt if the PPP felt it had been cheated.
But despite some tension in Jakarta, a city of more than 10 million, businesses were open and traffic was normal on Wednesday.

Political analysts blamed the violence on political rivalry, youthful exuberance and dissatisfaction and frustration with the government and system during an outpouring of political passion allowed only once every five years.

In his address, Suharto said the election would be "direct, free and secret". The election was not an end in itself, he added, "but an instrument and vehicle to adapt government policy and development with the wishes of the people as a whole".
He added that democracy could not be created overnight.
"Democracy is a long process of national development...it is not easy for any country to reach an ideal level of maturity in democracy, let alone a nation as complex as ours.
"Our complex society must remain united so it can build its strength to create a better life for all," he said.
